The first flight of a passenger Amphibian machine between Paris and London was made early this morning. "I can't think it's you speaking, Noll," she said. "Men—Englishmen feel so strongly about these matters. The difference of race is an overwhelming barrier. Nothing can be gained by attempting to break it down."
"My dear child, Peter is an extraordinary man. I have known him from a boy, and I can truthfully say that the barrier you speak of has already in his nature been practically broken down."

"Then you are mistaken, Noll," his sister retorted. "Indeed, you are. I can't explain, but I can feel it. And, listen!" She was suddenly moved to relate the incident of the miniature and the subtle changes that the Indian copyist had wrought in her face. "And he thinks it's like me," she concluded, raising her voice to accentuate the point, unanswerable and damning in her eyes. "Noll, he really thinks it's like me! And it makes me look like a little brown woman!"
Roland laughed at the indignation in her voice; but a moment later he was serious again.

"I can only repeat that I'm frightfully sorry, sisterkin," he said. His voice was kind, and there was no reproach in it, only infinite regret. "Not only are you refusing a wonderful position and a life such as is offered to few women, but you are practically making me a bankrupt."
"A bankrupt!" Hersée's voice was full of horror. "Only in gratitude," he replied, and the smile that curved his mobile lips was both pathetic and dignified.
"In gratitude! I don't understand. You've done far more for the Rajah than he has done for you."

PREPARING FOR TRANSATLANTIC FLIGHT.
Left to right: Captain Hugo Sundstedt of the Swedish Army and Lt. Nyegaard of the French Aviation Corps.

Captain Hugo Sundstadt arrived recently from France where he had been observing aerial developments for Sweden. The Captain is now in N.Y. but will leave next month for Florida to complete arrangements for the construction of an airplane which he will use in his attempt to cross the Atlantic.

The flight will probably be made in May. The machine will be ready by the middle of the end of February and two months will be spent making trial flights and in preparations. It was the Catpain's intention to bring a machine with him but it was impossible to get it made in Europe because of the war demands. He said that the Amper can made machines now compare very favorably with those of foreign manufacture.

The aviator must be something of a navigator so that he can act as his own pilot as the machine must fly above 12,000 feet because of air currents, prevailing any possibility of distinguishing ships and using them as guides. The machine will be a triplane and will have a width of approximately 130 feet and will require three propellers, with two motors of about 160 horses power such propeller. The Captain may fly the moving from Florida to St. Johns, Newfoundland, and will then wait for favorable weather and make the flight across the favorite to some point in Ireland. Later on he will go to France.
